One important correction to your theory: mounting through a loop device does **not** change the btrfs UUID or devid — those live inside the image data. Here's the full picture of filesystem `2f94843d` (the one you're trying to recover):

| devid | size | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 185 GiB, dev UUID `ec76422c-...` | **missing — this is the problem** |
| 2 | 201 GiB | ✅ complete image at `~/image.dd` |
| 3 | 100 GiB | `disk3.dd` truncated at 40G (sdc filled up), but 0 bytes of chunks are allocated on it — trivially fixable by sparse-padding |

Without devid 1, the filesystem can't be mounted at all — not even `-o ro,degraded` — because btrfs can't even read the chunk map. That's why every command reports "cannot read chunk root."

So everything hinges on finding devid 1: a **185 GiB device** (198,641,168,384 bytes — incidentally the exact same size as your root partition `sda3`). None of the current images match it: `/run/mount/image.dd` is the right size but contains your root fs, not this one — it looks like the wrong device may have been dd'd, or devid 1 was a 185 GiB disk/partition that's no longer attached (`/dev/sdb` was likely devid 2's source — its superblock is wiped but the size matches).

Do you know what physical disk or partition devid 1 was? If it still exists somewhere (another disk, an external drive, an image elsewhere), we can attach it and mount. If it's truly gone, the fallback is `btrfs rescue chunk-recover` against the surviving images to rebuild the chunk tree, then `btrfs restore` — only ~6.4 GiB was in use on this fs, so if metadata was RAID1 across devid 1 and 2 there's a real chance of getting files back, but I'd want your confirmation before running that since chunk-recover writes to the images (we'd work on copies, except sdc has almost no free space — we'd need to free some up first).

## The snapshot is very likely your missing devid 1

The missing device is exactly 198,641,168,384 bytes — the same size as this VPS's main partition (`sda3`). That fits a story where the old fs `2f94843d` used this VPS's own disk as devid 1, and it got wiped when the current OS (fsid `95cd48f0`) was installed over it. A snapshot from before that event would contain devid 1 intact. **Check the snapshot's creation date in the OVH panel** — your dd images were made May 24, so it needs to be from before whatever happened around then.

## Two things you must NOT do in the OVH panel

- **Do not click "Restore"** — that overwrites this VPS's live disk, destroying the current OS *and* `~/image.dd`, your only complete copy of devid 2.
- **Do not take a new snapshot** — VPS has one snapshot slot; a new one replaces the old one you need.

## How to get it

Per [OVH's snapshot guide](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-vps-using-snapshots?id=kb_article_view&sysparm_article=KB0047771), in the Control Panel: your VPS → Home tab → Snapshot tile → `…` menu → **Download the snapshot**. It generates a `curl`/`wget` command with a link valid 24 hours, delivering a **QCOW2** image. Your VPS range supports this (only legacy `vpsXXXX.ovh.us` machines don't). The panel shows the file size before you download. `qemu-img`/`qemu-nbd` are already installed here, so once it lands we can attach it read-only with `qemu-nbd`, locate the 185 GiB partition, and verify its superblock shows fsid `2f94843d` / devid 1 / dev UUID `ec76422c`. Then: sparse-pad `disk3.dd` to 100 GiB (costs no disk space), attach all three loops, and do a normal read-only mount.

## One problem: disk space

You have 17G free on `/` and zero on `/run/mount` (sdc). The QCOW2 will be compressed/sparse but a ~167 GiB-used disk likely produces a file far bigger than 17G. The biggest reclaimable item is **`/run/mount/image.dd` (59G)** — it's the truncated, weeks-old partial copy of your *current* root partition: wrong filesystem for this recovery, superseded by the live disk, and incomplete anyway. Deleting it frees enough room on sdc to receive the snapshot. There's also ~2.5G of repomix files in `~` if needed.

content.text:
Good question — your log clears this up. The May 24 TestDisk session was actually run against `/dev/sdb` (the 201G disk), and it found no valid partition table there — which makes sense, because sdb was a *whole-disk* btrfs member (devid 2), no GPT at all. That's why TestDisk only found garbage "EFI System" false positives. Imaging the whole of sdb is what produced `~/image.dd`, and that's why its size matches sdb exactly.

To your actual question — yes, imaging `/dev/sda3` and `/dev/sda` gives genuinely different files, but neither one changes any volume ID:

- **`/dev/sda3`** → the image starts directly at the btrfs filesystem. Byte 65536 of the file is the btrfs superblock. `blkid` on it (or its loop device) shows the filesystem UUID, and btrfs recognizes it immediately.
- **`/dev/sda`** → the image starts with the GPT partition table, then the EFI partition, then `/boot`, and the btrfs only begins ~15G in. `blkid` on that file shows `PTTYPE="gpt"` and *no filesystem UUID* — to reach the btrfs you'd need `losetup -P` (to expose the partitions as `loop0p3`) or an offset.

That difference is probably what made it *look* like loop mounting changes the volume ID — the whole-disk image just hides the filesystem behind a partition table. The UUID stored inside the filesystem never changes either way.

But here's the important implication for your recovery: `/run/mount/image.dd` was created from `sda3` on May 24, and it contains the **current** root filesystem (fsid `95cd48f0`) at generation 11696. So by May 24, `sda3` had already been overwritten with the new OS — devid 1 was already gone from that disk. No imaging of `sda` or `sda3`, then or now, can bring it back. The OVH snapshot from before the reinstall remains the only possible source of devid 1, which is why checking its creation date in the panel is the next move.

That settles it definitively. The scan found the filesystem UUID only inside devid 2's own two superblocks (at 64 KiB and 64 MiB) — **zero metadata tree blocks**. Combined with the earlier findings, the structure of the lost backup fs is now fully mapped:

- **devid 1** (the missing 185 GiB device): held the chunk tree *and* all filesystem metadata — directory structure, filenames, extent maps. This is why `chunk-recover` reported "no recoverable chunk" on May 30 and why nothing can mount, even degraded.
- **devid 2** (`~/image.dd`, complete): holds only raw file *content* — ~6.4 GiB of it, sitting between 1 and 8 GiB into the image.
- **devid 3** (`disk3.dd`): empty, never received any chunks; its truncation doesn't matter.

So your realistic options are now exactly two:

1. **The OVH snapshot** — the only path to a real mount with filenames and directory structure. If `vps-6aff90ab.vps.ovh.ca-snapshot` was taken on or before ~May 16–18 (before the current OS was installed over the old `sda3`, which the size evidence says was devid 1), it contains everything we're missing. Check its **creation date** in the OVH panel and, if it's old enough, generate the download link (Snapshot tile → `…` → Download the snapshot). Don't restore it and don't take a new snapshot — both would destroy what we're trying to save.

2. **File carving as a fallback** — if the snapshot turns out to be too recent, I can run `photorec`-style carving over the 1–8 GiB data region of `~/image.dd`. That recovers file contents but no filenames or paths, and won't work well if the backup fs used compression. Worth doing only if option 1 falls through.

The snapshot date is the one fact that decides everything — can you check it in the panel?

That rules out the snapshot — after the reinstall, devid 1's metadata was already gone, so the snapshot contains nothing we don't already have. We're down to carving the ~6.4 GiB of raw file content out of `~/image.dd`. Whether that's worthwhile depends on what the data looks like (plain files carve well; btrfs-compressed extents carve poorly), so let me sample it first:
